title: Economic foundations: resources, scarcity and business ownership
objective: Explain scarcity and the factors of production, distinguish goods from services and economic systems, and compare the major forms of business ownership.
body:
Every business decision starts with one economic fact: **scarcity**. Resources are limited, but human wants are unlimited, so people, businesses and governments must make choices. Every choice has an **opportunity cost**, the value of the next-best alternative given up. If a student spends Saturday working a shift instead of attending a robotics workshop, the workshop is the opportunity cost, not the money earned.

**Factors of production.** Economists group the resources used to make goods and services into four categories:
- **Land**: natural resources such as soil, water, timber and oil.
- **Labor**: human effort, both physical and mental, paid with wages.
- **Capital**: tools, machinery and buildings used to produce other goods (not money itself in the economic sense).
- **Entrepreneurship**: the initiative to combine the other three and take on risk in pursuit of profit.

Businesses produce **goods**, which are tangible products, and **services**, which are intangible activities such as a haircut or tax preparation. Services cannot be stored, and their quality often depends on the person delivering them.

**Economic systems.** Societies answer the questions of what to produce, how to produce it and for whom in different ways. In a **market economy**, private individuals own resources and prices set by supply and demand guide decisions. In a **command economy**, the government owns most resources and plans production. A **traditional economy** relies on custom. Most real nations, including the United States, run a **mixed economy** that combines private markets with government regulation and public services.

**Forms of ownership.** A business owner must choose a legal structure.
1. A **sole proprietorship** is owned by one person. It is easy to start and the owner keeps all profits, but the owner has **unlimited liability**, meaning personal assets can be taken to pay business debts.
2. A **partnership** has two or more owners who share profits, skills and, in a general partnership, unlimited liability.
3. A **corporation** is a separate legal entity owned by stockholders. Owners enjoy **limited liability**, but the business faces more regulation and, for a C corporation, profits can be taxed twice: once at the corporate level and again when paid out as dividends.
4. A **limited liability company (LLC)** blends limited liability with flexible, pass-through taxation.

The most common mistake students make is treating opportunity cost as every option given up or as the money spent. It is only the single next-best alternative. A close second is calling money a factor of production; in economics, capital means the physical tools used to produce.
examples: A bakery's ovens and mixers are capital, the flour and water come from land, the bakers provide labor, and the owner who opened the shop supplies entrepreneurship.
Two friends open a landscaping business as a general partnership; when a client sues over property damage, both partners' personal savings can be at risk.

questions.stem: Maya can either babysit for $60 on Friday or attend a paid coding camp session she values more than babysitting or anything else. She chooses the camp. What is her opportunity cost?
choices: The $60 she would have earned babysitting
The cost of the coding camp session
Every activity she could have done Friday
Nothing, because she chose her preferred option
questions.explanation: Opportunity cost is the next-best alternative given up, which is babysitting and its $60. The camp fee is the price of her choice, not what she sacrificed.

questions.stem: A pizza shop buys a new conveyor oven. Which factor of production does the oven represent?
questions.explanation: Capital is the tools and equipment used to produce other goods. Land would be the natural resources, such as the wheat in the flour, not a manufactured oven.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a service rather than a good?
questions.explanation: Car detailing is an intangible activity performed for a customer. Potting soil is tangible, so it is a good even though it comes from natural resources.

questions.stem: Jordan wants to start a mobile phone repair business alone, keep all profits and avoid complex paperwork. Which ownership form best fits?
questions.explanation: A sole proprietorship is the simplest form for one owner and keeps all profits with that owner. A corporation offers limited liability but requires much more formation paperwork.

questions.stem: A country's government decides how many tractors factories will build and sets their prices. What type of economic system is this?
questions.explanation: Central government planning of production and prices defines a command economy. A market economy lets supply and demand, not officials, set prices.

questions.stem: Why do many entrepreneurs form an LLC instead of a sole proprietorship?
choices: It eliminates all taxes on profits
It protects owners' personal assets while allowing pass-through taxation
It allows the business to sell stock on a public exchange
questions.explanation: An LLC offers limited liability with flexible pass-through taxation. It does not eliminate taxes; profits are still taxed on the owners' returns.

questions.stem: A C corporation earns profit, pays corporate income tax, then pays dividends that stockholders report as income. This is called:
questions.explanation: Profit taxed at the corporate level and again as shareholder dividends is double taxation. Pass-through taxation is the opposite, where profit is taxed only once on owners' returns.

questions.stem: The United States has private businesses but also government regulations, public schools and Social Security. This best describes a:
questions.explanation: A mix of private markets and government involvement is a mixed economy. A pure market economy would have little or no government role in these areas.

flashcards.definition: The condition in which limited resources cannot satisfy unlimited wants, forcing choices.
The value of the next-best alternative given up when making a choice.
Tools, machinery and buildings used to produce other goods and services.
Owner responsibility for business debts that extends to personal assets.
An economic system combining private markets with government regulation and services.
